context.full_target:
A sphere-valued map cannot vanish outside a compact set. As approved by
the user on 2026-10-23, interpret spatial compact support as compact support
of a perturbation from a **fixed unit vector**, locally uniformly in time.
This is a disclosed nontrivial interpretation, not a claimed author-issued
correction.

Let \(n,m\geq1\) be integers and let
\(u:\mathbb R^n\times(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R^m\) be jointly smooth.
Fix \(q\in\mathbb R^m\) with \(|q|=1\). Assume:

1. \(|u(x,t)|=1\) for all \(x\) and \(t>0\).
2. The acceleration \(u_{tt}-\Delta_xu\) is normal to the sphere at
   \(u\): at each point there is a real scalar \(a(x,t)\) with
   \(u_{tt}-\Delta_xu=a u\). No regularity of the selected scalar is
   assumed.
3. For every \(0<s<t<\infty\), a compact set
   \(C_{[s,t]}\subset\mathbb R^n\) exists such that \(u(x,r)=q\) for
   \(x\notin C_{[s,t]}\), \(r\in[s,t]\).

With Euclidean norms and Lebesgue measure, define

\[
e(x,t)=|u_t(x,t)|^2+\sum_{j=1}^n|\partial_{x_j}u(x,t)|^2,
\qquad E(t)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}e(x,t)\,dx.
\]

The spatial gradient square is the Frobenius square, and
\(\Delta_xu=\sum_j\partial_{x_jx_j}u\) component by component.
Prove integrability of \(e(\cdot,t)\), differentiability of \(E\),
and \(E'(t)=0\) for every \(t>0\). No assertion at time zero is required.
context.conclusion: For every t>0, the density e(·,t) is Lebesgue integrable on R^n, E is differentiable at t, and E'(t)=0. In particular E(t)=E(s) for all s,t>0. The density is |u_t|^2+sum_{j=1}^n|∂_{x_j}u|^2 with Euclidean norms, and E(t) is its spatial Lebesgue integral, with no factor 1/2. No assertion at time zero is made.

record.definition: For x in R^n and t>0, Δ_xu(x,t)=sum_{j=1}^n ∂_{x_jx_j}u(x,t), component by component. The notation u_t,u_tt,∂_{x_j}u and ∂_{x_j}u_t denotes the corresponding classical partial derivatives on R^n×(0,∞). D_xu is the m-by-n matrix with columns ∂_{x_j}u, and |D_xu|^2 is its Frobenius square sum_{j=1}^n |∂_{x_j}u|^2. Vectors have the Euclidean dot product and norm. Spatial integrals are Lebesgue integrals on R^n; boxes carry the restricted Lebesgue measure. int denotes topological interior and 1_A denotes the indicator of a set A.
e(x,t)=|u_t(x,t)|^2+sum_{j=1}^n |∂_{x_j}u(x,t)|^2, for x in R^n and t>0, with exactly the Euclidean and Frobenius normalization of problem.md:38-46.
For every t>0, E(t)=∫_{R^n} e(x,t) dx. This is the ordinary finite Lebesgue integral, used after spatial integrability has been established; there is no factor 1/2.

record.statement: For every x∈R^n and t>0, u(x,t)·u_t(x,t)=0 and u_t(x,t)·(u_tt(x,t)-Δ_xu(x,t))=0. Moreover u·u_tt=-|u_t|^2 and u·∂_{x_jx_j}u=-|∂_{x_j}u|^2 for every 1≤j≤n. Every real a satisfying u_tt-Δ_xu=a u at that point equals sum_{j=1}^n|∂_{x_j}u|^2-|u_t|^2; thus u_tt-Δ_xu=(sum_{j=1}^n|∂_{x_j}u|^2-|u_t|^2)u.

record.statement: For every t0>0, put J=[t0/2,3t0/2]. There exist a compact C⊂R^n and R>0 with C⊂(-R,R)^n such that u(x,r)=q for every x∉C and r∈J. Put Q=[-R,R]^n; its Lebesgue measure is (2R)^n<∞. Every positive-order partial derivative of u is zero on (R^n\C)×int J. For each r∈int J the following scalar spatial functions are continuous, bounded on Q, zero outside C, and Lebesgue integrable on R^n: e(·,r), e_t(·,r), u_t·u_tt, u_t·∂_{x_j}u, ∂_{x_j}u_t·∂_{x_j}u, u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u, and ∂_{x_j}(u_t·∂_{x_j}u), for each 1≤j≤n. Consequently e(·,t) is Lebesgue integrable for every t>0.
